rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وعلي بن الحسين وقتادة وأبو العالية وعطاء وابن جبير ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان وجعفر الصادق
rows.claim: These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Meccan; Abū Ḥayyān says the claim is supported by the seven oft-repeated verses being mentioned in a Meccan sūra.
rows.anchor: قال علي ،   وابن عباس ،   وعلي بن الحسين ،   وقتادة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وعطاء بن يسار ومجاهد وسواد بن زياد والزهري وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Medinan, contrary to the Meccan attribution.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو هريرة ،   وعطاء بن يسار ،   ومجاهد ،   وسواد بن زياد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view calls al-Fātiḥa both Meccan and Medinan.
rows.anchor: هي مدنية ،   وقيل إنها مكية مدنية

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from Ubay identifies al-Fātiḥa as the seven oft-repeated verses and one of the seven long sūras, revealed some time after al-Ḥijr.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي : إنها السبع المثاني والسبع الطوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer was prescribed in Mecca, and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف أن فرض الصلاة كان بمكة ،   وما حفظ أنه كانت في الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ has uses for attachment, instrument, oath, cause, circumstance, location, and transfer; Abū Ḥayyān illustrates each with Arabic examples.
rows.anchor: باء الجر تأتي لمعان : للإلصاق ،   والاستعانة ،   والقسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other uses of bāʾ include emphasis, substitution, exchange, separation, and superiority, each supported with an example.
rows.anchor: وتأتي زائدة للتوكيد : شربن بماء البحر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some grammarians call circumstantial bāʾ accompaniment, add a causal sense, subsume instrument under cause, and explain circumstantial bāʾ as “with.”
rows.anchor: وكنى بعضهم عن الحال بالمصاحبة ،   وزاد فيها كونها للتعليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ism is reported with several forms, while the Basrans derive it from s-m-w and the Kufans from w-s-m; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the Basran derivation.
rows.anchor: والبصري يقول : مادته سين وميم وواو

rows.speaker: الكوفي
rows.claim: The Kufan derivation makes the root of ism w-s-m, whereas Abū Ḥayyān prefers the Basran s-m-w analysis.
rows.anchor: والكوفي يقول : واو وسين وميم ،   والأرجح الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians assign al- uses including particular or generic reference, presence, evocation of a quality, predominance, relative meaning, and fixed or nonfixed augmentation.
rows.anchor: الاستدلال في كتب النحو : أل للعهد في شخص أو جنس ،   وللحضور

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most authorities consider Allāh a proper name for the true deity only, originally un-derived.
rows.anchor: علم لا يطلق إلا على المعبود بحق مرتجل غير مشتق عند الأكثرين

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق وأبو عمر والنضر والمبرد
rows.claim: Competing derivations connect Allāh to rising, concealment, fear, bewilderment, worship, or rest; Abū Ḥayyān reports these without choosing among them.
rows.anchor: من أله أي فزع ،   قاله ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: الخليل والقناد
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and al-Qannād derive Allāh from w-l-h, “to be transported with delight,” with hamza substituted for wāw; Abū Ḥayyān calls the proposal weak.
rows.anchor: من وله ،   أي طرب ،   وأبدلت الهمزة فيه من الواو نحو أشاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural āliha can be parsed as faʿāl with a passive meaning, like kitāb meaning “written.”
rows.anchor: وقولهم في الجمع آلهة ،   وتكون فعالا بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Allāh derives from al-ilāh, al- marks predominance: ilāh can name true or false deities, while Allāh names only the true deity; the comparison to al-Najm is challenged.
rows.anchor: وأل في الله إذا قلنا أصله الإله ،   قالوا للغلبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the other proposed derivations, al- is an inseparable extra article; omitting it in lāh abūka is anomalous.
rows.anchor: فأل فيه زائدة لازمة ،   وشذ حذفها في قولهم لاه أبوك

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي والسهيلي
rows.claim: They say al- is part of Allāh and the hamza became connective through frequent use; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because the resulting form would be fʿāl and would not explain the lack of tanwīn.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن أل في الله من نفس الكلمة ،   ووصلت الهمزة لكثرة الاستعمال

rows.speaker: أبو يزيد البلخي
rows.claim: Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī calls Allāh a foreign word, citing Jewish and Christian lāhā and saying Arabs adopted and changed it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو يزيد البلخي : هو أعجمي ،   فإن اليهود والنصارى يقولون لاها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported view treats Allāh as an attribute rather than a personal name because God is not sensed or immediately apprehended and is known through His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this unusual.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب ما قيل في الله أنه صفة وليس اسم ذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final alif in Allāh is variously said to be omitted to distinguish its spelling from lāhū, to lighten it, or because of a spelling convention.
rows.anchor: وحذفت الألف الأخيرة من الله لئلا يشكل بخط اللاه اسم الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raḥmān is an intensive faʿlān form from mercy, with al- marking predominance; it is used only of God, like His proper name.
rows.anchor: { الرحمن } : فعلان من الرحمة ،   وأصل بنائه من اللازم

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab reports the unusual claim that raḥmān is foreign, with its khāʾ adapted to Arabic ḥāʾ.
rows.anchor: أعجمي بالخاء المعجمة فعرب بالحاء ،   قاله ثعلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl form; faʿīl is one of the five standard intensive patterns, with some grammarians adding another faʿīl pattern.
rows.anchor: { الرحيم } : فعيل محول من فاعل للمبالغة ،   وهو أحد الأمثلة الخمسة

rows.speaker: العملس بن عقيل
rows.claim: The poet al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl uses raḥīm to mean marḥūm, “one shown mercy.”
rows.anchor: وقيل : وجاء رحيم بمعنى مرحوم ،   قال العملس بن عقيل

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans parse the bāʾ as instrumental and the phrase as accusative with an implied “I begin”; they posit that implied verb for acts begun with the formula.
rows.anchor: الباء في بسم الله للاستعانة ،   نحو كتبت بالقلم ،   وموضعها نصب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as “I read” or “I recite,” and claims fronting yields exclusivity; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the latter claim.
rows.anchor: وقدره الزمخشري فعلا غير بدأت وجعله متأخرا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says fronting an object is good Arabic just as ordinary order is; Abū Ḥayyān cites this against the claim that fronting necessarily entails exclusivity.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه : وقد تكلم على ضربت زيدا ما نصه

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basrans parse ism as nominative in an implied nominal sentence, approximately “my beginning is fixed/stable in the name of God”; Abū Ḥayyān weighs this against the verbal parse.
rows.anchor: وقيل موضع اسم رفع التقدير ابتدائي ثابت ،   أو مستقر باسم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ism is a conventional word denoting an existent, perceptible or intelligible, without marking time; its referent is the named thing, while naming makes the word a sign for that meaning.
rows.anchor: والاسم هو اللفظ الدال بالوضع على موجود في العيان ،   إن كان محسوسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the word, its referent, and the act of naming; a judgment attributed literally to a name can instead use “name” metaphorically for its referent.
rows.anchor: فقد اتضحت المباينة بين الاسم والمسمى والتسمية

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī reads “glorify the name of your Lord” as an insertion directing people to glorify the Lord and ensuring remembrance includes spoken utterance as well as inward recollection.
rows.anchor: وقد تأول السهيلي ،   رحمه الله ،   قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī explains “you worship only names” as a metaphor for idols with false, unreal names, so their worship is effectively worship of invented names.
rows.anchor: بأنها أسماء كاذبة غير واقعة على حقيقة

rows.speaker: الكسائي والأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif in bi-sm with other divine names; al-Farrāʾ restricts deletion to the full basmala.
rows.anchor: فقال الكسائي والأخفش : تحذف الألف

rows.speaker: الأعلم
rows.claim: Al-Aʿlam treats raḥmān as a proper name and therefore appositional rather than adjectival, citing its independent use in other verses.
rows.anchor: وذهب الأعلم وغيره إلى أنه بدل ،   وزعم أن الرحمن علم

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī rejects apposition and explanatory apposition because Allāh needs no clarification; raḥmān is an epithet of praise, though it can function like a proper name.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد السهيلي : البدل فيه عندي ممتنع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says the two names are synonymous; another distinguishes them, making raḥmān more emphatic and encompassing major blessings while raḥīm completes it with subtle blessings.
rows.anchor: قيل دلالتهما واحد نحو ندمان ونديم ،   وقيل معناهما مختلف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors raḥmān for foundational blessings and raḥīm as a complement for finer, subtler blessings.
rows.anchor: ليكون كالتتمة والرديف ليتناول ما دق منها ولطف ،   واختاره الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān holds that the names intensify mercy in different ways, so their combination is not mere repetition: faʿlān suggests fullness or dominance, while faʿīl suggests repeated occurrence at objects of mercy.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن جهة المبالغة مختلفة ،   فلذلك جمع بينهما ،   فلا يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intensive forms differ in transitivity: faʿlān does not take an object, whereas faʿīl does, like an active participle.
rows.anchor: ولذلك لا يتعدى فعلان ،   ويتعدى فعيل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid distinguishes the names as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد : رحمن الدنيا ورحيم الآخرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the same distinction; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be accepted if sound.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : « الرحمن رحمن الدنيا

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī gives the reverse allocation: raḥmān for the next life and raḥīm for this life.
rows.anchor: وقال القرطبي : رحمن الآخرة ورحيم الدنيا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the two names concern the inhabitants of heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك : لأهل السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima distinguishes one mercy from one hundred mercies.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة : برحمة واحدة وبمائة رحمة

rows.speaker: المزني
rows.claim: Al-Muzanī distinguishes blessings of worldly life from blessings of religion.
rows.anchor: وقال المزني : بنعمة الدنيا والدين

rows.speaker: العزيزي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīzī assigns raḥmān to universal gifts such as rain and the senses, and raḥīm to believers through guidance and divine care.
rows.anchor: وقال العزيزي : الرحمن بجميع خلقه

rows.speaker: المحاسبي
rows.claim: Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.
rows.anchor: وقال المحاسبي : برحمة النفوس ورحمة القلوب

rows.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh relates the names to needs of the afterlife and worldly life.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن معاذ : لمصالح المعاد والمعاش

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq says the generally framed name concerns provision broadly, while the specially framed name concerns forgiveness for believers.
rows.anchor: وقال الصادق : خاص اللفظ بصيغة عامة في الرزق

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab says raḥmān is more emphatic in praise and raḥīm is gentler.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب : الرحمن أمدح ،   والرحيم ألطف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says raḥmān gives blessings of kinds humans cannot provide, while raḥīm gives blessings of kinds humans can provide.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الرحمن المنعم بما لا يتصور جنسه من العباد

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says raḥmān covers every kind of mercy and belongs uniquely to God, while raḥīm concerns believers, as in 33:43.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي : الرحمن اسم عام في جميع أنواع الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine mercy may figuratively mean beneficence, an attribute of action; another view defines it as willing good, an attribute of essence, raising the dispute over whether attributes of action are originated or eternal.
rows.anchor: ووصف الله تعالى بالرحمة مجاز عن إنعامه على عباده

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some theologians define divine mercy as God's will to bring good to whomever He wills, making it an attribute of essence.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم : هي إرادة الخير لمن أراد الله تعالى به ذلك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Human mercy is defined either as tenderness in the heart or as intending good or averting harm, since one can help another without feeling tenderness.
rows.anchor: وأما الرحمة التي من العباد فقيل هي رقة تحدث في القلب

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī rejects the idea that omitting the verb merely lightens speech: omission keeps God's name first and matches utterance to the heart's intention to remember only God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو القاسم السهيلي : وليس كما زعموا ،   إذ لو كان

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī compares this ellipsis with “God is greatest,” whose unstated completion lets the wording match the heart's intended exclusivity.
rows.anchor: كما تقول في الصلاة الله أكبر ،   ومعناه من كل شيء ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is omitted in writing in bi-sm Allāh and in raḥmān because of frequent use.
rows.anchor: ومن الحذف أيضا حذف الألف في بسم الله وفي الرحمن في الخط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating descriptive epithets can magnify the one described or reinforce the meaning until it settles in the mind.
rows.anchor: النوع الثاني : التكرار في الوصف ،   ويكون إما لتعظيم الموصوف

rows.speaker: قوم من الكوفيين
rows.claim: Some Kufans pause after raḥīm with its mīm quiescent, then begin al-ḥamdu with a cut hamza.
rows.anchor: قرأ قوم من الكوفيين بسكون الميم ،   ويقفون عليها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority connect raḥīm to al-ḥamdu, retaining the genitive ending and joining the following hamza.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على جر الميم ووصل الألف من الحمد

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reports a Bedouin reading with an opened mīm and connected hamza, explained as transferring the hamza's vowel to the mīm before elision.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنه يقرأ الرحيم الحمد بفتح الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd is verbal praise of beauty, for a blessing or otherwise, and its opposite is blame; it is not a reversal of madḥ, since madḥ can apply to inanimate things.
rows.anchor: { الحمد } الثناء على الجميل من نعمة أو غيرها باللسان وحده

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī treats ḥamd as an inversion of madḥ; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because a jewel may be praised but not thanked.
rows.anchor: خلافا لابن الأنباري ،   إذ هما في التصريفات متساويان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Views say ḥamd and shukr are synonymous, ḥamd is broader, or shukr praises God's acts while ḥamd praises His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān prefers ḥamd as broader.
rows.anchor: والحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد ،   أو الحمد أعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām can express possession, transfer of ownership, entitlement, relation, cause, communication, exclamation, specification, result, location, endpoint, and superiority; Qur'anic and Arabic examples illustrate these functions.
rows.anchor: اللام : للملك وشبهه ،   وللتمليك وشبهه ،   وللاستحقاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can mean master, owner, constant one, deity, or reformer; some add “companion,” supported by a poem about the master of the dogs.
rows.anchor: { رب العالمين } الرب : السيد ،   والمالك ،   والثابت

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some lexicographers allow rabb to mean “companion,” adducing a poem in which a man approaches as master of the dogs.
rows.anchor: وزاد بعضهم بمعنى الصاحب ،   مستدلا بقوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās defines al-ʿālamīn as every being with a soul.
rows.anchor: ومدلوله كل ذي روح ،   قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: البجلي
rows.claim: Al-Bajalī says al-ʿālamīn means people.
rows.anchor: أو الناس ،   قاله البجلي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās specifies humans, jinn, and angels.
rows.anchor: أو الإنس والجن والملائكة ،   قاله أيضا ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والفراء
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ include humans, jinn, angels, and devils among al-ʿālamīn.
rows.anchor: أو الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين ،   قاله أبو عبيدة والفراء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-ʿālamīn means the two classes of moral beings, humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: أو الثقلان ،   قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: أبو معاذ
rows.claim: Abū Muʿādh restricts al-ʿālamīn to the children of Adam.
rows.anchor: أو بنو آدم ،   قاله أبو معاذ

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq defines al-ʿālamīn as the people of Paradise and the Fire.
rows.anchor: أو أهل الجنة والنار ،   قاله الصادق

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says al-ʿālamīn means those who receive provision.
rows.anchor: أو المرتزقون ،   قاله عبد الرحمن بن زيد

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda define al-ʿālamīn as every created thing.
rows.anchor: أو كل مصنوع ،   قاله الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation restricts al-ʿālamīn to spiritual beings.
rows.anchor: أو الروحانيون ،   قاله بعضهم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read al-ḥamdu with ḍamma on the dāl. Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla assimilates its mīm to the following lām; al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's, a stranger assimilation.
rows.anchor: والجمهور قرأوا بضم دال الحمد

rows.speaker: الحسن وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's kasra; the author calls this stranger because a case vowel follows a non-case vowel.
rows.anchor: كما أتبع الحسن وزيد بن علي كسرة الدال لكسرة اللام

rows.speaker: هارون العتكي ورؤبة وسفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Hārūn al-ʿAtakī, Ruʾba, and Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna read al-ḥamda in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ هارون العتكي ،   ورؤبة ،   وسفيان بن عيينة الحمد بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article in al-ḥamd may be anaphoric, defining the familiar praise; essential, defining the nature; or generic, encompassing all praises. A verbal noun is ordinarily not pluralized.
rows.anchor: والحمد مصدر معرف بأل ،   إما للعهد ،   أي الحمد المعروف بينكم لله

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the plural aḥmad for ḥamd, apparently treating its different kinds as distinct, and cites a poem using aḥmadī.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن الأعرابي : جمعه على أحمد

rows.speaker: القراء السبعة
rows.claim: The nominative reading is stronger and agreed upon by the seven canonical readers: it states that praise is established and enduringly belongs to God, including praise by God and others.
rows.anchor: وقراءة الرفع أمكن في المعنى ،   ولهذا أجمع عليها السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With nominative al-ḥamdu the lām marks entitlement; with accusative al-ḥamda a verb such as “I praise God” must be supplied, conveying renewed action.
rows.anchor: ومعنى اللام في لله الاستحقاق ،   ومن نصب ،   فلا بد من عامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the accusative reading, Abū Ḥayyān prefers an omitted verb directly indicated by the wording, such as “I praise God,” over “I say” or “adhere to praise.”
rows.anchor: والأول هو الصحيح لدلالة اللفظ عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the accusative reading the lām is explanatory, not a strengthening of transitivity, since the verbal noun cannot govern this phrase as its object.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة النصب ،   اللام للتبيين ،   كما قال أعني لله

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي وطائفة
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a group read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise; the reading weakens if the following adjectives remain genitive.
rows.anchor: قرأ زيد بن علي وطائفة { رب العالمين } بالنصب على المدح

rows.speaker: الأهوازي
rows.claim: Al-Ahwāzī reports Zayd ibn ʿAlī reading rabb, raḥmān, and raḥīm all in the accusative, avoiding the mismatch in case.
rows.anchor: على أن الأهوازي حكى في قراءة زيد بن علي أنه قرأ { رب العالمين ،   الرحمن الرحيم } بنصب الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects parsing accusative rabb as an implied verb of praise or as apposition: one rests on imagined syntax, the other is interrupted by raḥmān raḥīm.
rows.anchor: وقول من زعم أنه نصب رب بفعل دل عليه الكلام قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb may be a verbal noun used adjectivally or an active participle with deleted alif; as a title it is exclusive to God, while others require a possessive complement.
rows.anchor: ورب مصدر وصف به على أحد وجوه الوصف بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article in al-ʿālamīn is exhaustive; ʿālam is an irregular collective and its sound masculine plural is even more irregular because it violates some conditions of that pattern.
rows.anchor: وأل في العالمين للاستغراق ،   وجمع العالم شاذ لأنه اسم جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers that al-ʿālamīn denote morally responsible beings, supported by the verse about signs for the knowledgeable; Ḥafṣ's kasra on the lām clarifies the sense.
rows.anchor: والذي أختاره أنه ينطلق على المكلفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raḥmān and raḥīm, already discussed in the basmala, and rabb al-ʿālamīn are praise epithets following the unique divine name.
rows.anchor: { الرحمن الرحيم } تقدم الكلام عليهما في البسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence begins with lordship; when rabb means master, owner, or deity, God's control makes mercy the fitting next description, sustaining hope of pardon after error.
rows.anchor: وبدأ أولا بالوصف بالربوبية ،   فإن كان الرب بمعنى السيد ،   أو بمعنى المالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb cannot mean “the constant one” or “companion,” because neither sense can be annexed to al-ʿālamīn; if it means “reformer,” mercy implies little need for reform, since compassion motivates reform.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح أن يكون الرب بمعى الثابت ،   ولا بمعنى الصاحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever is characterized by lordship and mercy toward those under His care is deserving of praise.
rows.anchor: إن من كان موصوفا بالربوبية والرحمة للمربوبين كان مستحقا للحمد

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the two epithets in the genitive as adjectives; apposition and explanatory apposition are also proposed parses.
rows.anchor: وخفض الرحمن الرحيم الجمهور ،   ونصبهما أبو العالية

rows.speaker: أبو العالية وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمرو
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read raḥmān and raḥīm in the accusative as detached praise.
rows.anchor: ونصبهما أبو العالية وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمرو

rows.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني
rows.claim: Abū Razīn al-ʿUqaylī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, and Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī read the epithets in the nominative, also as detached praise.
rows.anchor: ورفعهما أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive can be adjectival, appositional, or explanatory; nominative and accusative readings detach the words from the preceding construction.
rows.anchor: فالخفض على النعت ،   وقيل في الخفض إنه بدل أو عطف بيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa, repeating raḥmān and raḥīm underscores the greatness of these attributes and reinforces them.
rows.anchor: وفي تكرار الرحمن الرحيم إن كانت التسمية آية من الفاتحة

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī argues that repetition proves the basmala is not a verse of al-Fātiḥa: adjacent verses of the same meaning do not occur without a separating cadence, and he says al-ḥamdu does not really separate them.
rows.anchor: وجعل مكي تكرارها دليلا على أن التسمية ليست بآية من الفاتحة

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī proposes reading the sequence as “praise belongs to God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, Lord of the worlds,” placing mercy beside praise and kingship beside kingship.
rows.anchor: تقديره الحمد لله ،   الرحمن الرحيم ،   رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls Makkī's argument defective and defends the Qur'anic order: lordship and mercy precede dominion on Judgment Day and worship, pairing lordship with dominion and mercy with worship.
rows.anchor: والترتيب القرآني جاء في غاية الفصاحة لأنه تعالى وصف نفسه بصفة الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes classify pauses as complete, sufficient, improper, and other kinds, with books arranged by sūra; Abū Ḥayyān says knowledge of Arabic makes these manuals unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر المفسرون في علم التفسير الوقف ،   وقد اختلف في أقسامه
